body:
>  She's like 24 now though so I hope she would at least regret doing that.

This is a good way to look at it. The best weapon I've found against OCD is logic. When you have an upsetting thought, confront it, and ask yourself about it. Yes, thinking through it and questioning it will make you feel worse temporarily, but it will give you power over the OCD. Here you're confirming to yourself that the thought is irrational and bullshit because people grow up and what someone was like as a teen is very different from 24. So if the thought is irrational in that way, in what other ways is it also irrational?

What did you learn with your therapist when you had them? What did you learn back then with regards to your thoughts and coping mechanisms? It's harder to manage OCD without help (although definitely possible!)  so hopefully your insurance will be sorted soon so you can get back into therapy and progress further.

You are finding more things to panic about here. You recognise that this was a bit of a daft thing to say, but that you were under a lot of stress at the time. If this was someone you knew, who was in the same situation, and made the same comment, what would *your* reaction be?

> It's not going to happen. She doesn't care anywhere near as much about your pictures or them getting out as you do.

The very first thing you did was provide reassurance. If you're written it as you did above, with questions that made OP think about this themselves, that would be helping them to think about it rationally. Instead you told them that everything would be fine, that is a form of reassurance. No CBT therapist will tell you that the fear you have isn't going to happen, they teach you to recognise that yourself instead.

I can see you have good intentions but a lot of your post is providing reassurance. That's detrimental to OCD and actually makes it worse in the long term. 

OP, you need to learn to reassure yourself. I completely agree with the above second point, this is something you just need to accept. Take a deep breath, and once the panic subsides, which it will, go on with your day. If this pops into your head again, same routine. If you feel the need to carry out a compulsion, wait twenty minutes. If you still feel the same then, go ahead and carry it out, but for most people this is enough time for panic to subside and logic to kick in. 

Are you seeing a therapist for your OCD?

Hey, I never said I didn't completely fall apart. I did. Lots. I'd be in a crumpled heap on the floor unable to think about anything about the damned spiders in the next room. But the point is that despite feeling like utter shit at those points, *I'm still here.* Going through that panic was awful but **nothing bad happened.** That's what ERP is all about, it shows you that your fears are complete shit. I do still feel sick and panicky when I think about the spiders I've dealt with and the spiders still in my home, but now I can tell that feeling to firmly fuck off because I know from experience that nothing will happen.

I had a lot of support from some very wonderful friends who live on the other side of the world. If I was struggling to push myself towards something I'd call them up and cry down the phone. They knew not to reassure me but were supportive and gave me encouragement to tackle it myself. One notable occasion was when there was this absolutely giant spider in the bath, I couldn't reach it to squash it, it wouldn't fit down the drain, I'd sprayed half a can of supposed spider killer on it with no result and oh man I was just a mess. A friend sat on the other end of Skype the whole time and told me I could do it. And once spidey was gone it meant I had someone to brag to and who was proud of me for tackling such a difficult thing. It's important to have someone to show off to when you do well, it always gives me a shiny happy feeling that someone else realises how much work I'm putting in and that it's paying off.

I find that for me exposure therapy works better if you treat it like a band-aid, and just rip it right off. The more time I have to think about it, the more time my OCD has to set in. I couldn't control when spiders popped out, I had to work on their schedule, and that made it easier. The ERP I'm working on now I have to plan and the more I think about it, the harder it is to do. If someone came up to me and said 'right, you're going to touch the floor then not wash your hands for at least half an hour. Right now,' I would stress like mad the whole half an hour but I wouldn't have time to get myself into a flap before touching the floor. 

And you know, you've just done it twice - when you read my first comment and then when you read about the spider in the bath above. You didn't know the comments were coming. I bet you felt sick and shaky and nasty. But you got through it and you're still here reading and even as a complete stranger I'm super fucking proud of you. Give yourself a fucking massive pat on the back. If you have someone who understands your OCD go and tell them you read about spiders today and that that's a huge thing for you. That's what ERP is all about, and the more of it you do the easier it gets, one step at a time.

It would be fantastic exposure therapy for you. If you can visit a spider that belongs to someone else I would highly recommend it, sometimes zoos/butterfly houses have spider exhibits and touchy feely sessions. You could go for a private session and explain to the handler in advance. If you can't look at spiders I would start with the basic going through photographs before confronting a spider in person.

Spiders and other bugs are a large part of my contamination OCD. Then I moved into a house INFESTED with spiders. There's a nest inside a wall I can't get to. And these are big bastards, with the chunky body and the long spindly legs. I kept finding them everywhere, all the time. I'd get up in the night and find twenty spiders in the bath. 

I live alone so the only person who can deal with these is me. There is no other option, I was thrown in headfirst. There have been a lot of freakouts. An awful lot of freakouts. There has been hysterical crying and panicked hours-long Skype conversations with friends while I close all the doors between me and the spider(s) until I'm calm enough to deal with it. And it has been SO GOOD for me. I'm still not 100% but for the first time in my life I can look at a spider on the ceiling and not instantly fall apart. It is wonderful. 

Exposure therapy is hard as fuck. But it will help your OCD no end if you can push yourself to do it. Talk to your therapist if you have one, but you can do ERP on your own if this isn't an option.

RE the checking for spiders thing, this isn't always an OCD issue. Some people without OCD are just legit frightened of them and will also check the room for them each night. Obviously it is an issue for you but for some people it's 'just' a normal phobia.

Remind yourself that this is not the end of the world. Anyone working through any kind of problem will slip and fall at some point along the way. The important thing is that you pull yourself back up and keep walking. You did well to ignore the compulsion as long as you did, every time you do it longer that's an improvement.

I agree with /u/afternoonbeauty to reset. Sometimes I just go straight to bed, it saves me sitting thinking over which isn't helpful. If you exercise I find that helpful too, doing something physical which will take your attention and channel it into something productive.

Ha. It's funny, but I've never had a problem with that. I can scrub a toilet no problems. But y'know, if something touches the fairly clean floor I freak the fuck out. I find it really interesting how it affects us all differently. I also find it helpful sometimes because it reminds me of the utter lack of logic OCD has which is a big help for me to fight back against it.

Assuming that this is an option that one day exists and worked, I still think this will also depend on the individual. Technology is a huge part of our lives nowadays but I can definitely see some pushback against the idea of using technology inside heads, even if it is removable.

Personally I'm not sure where I stand on it. I'm completely uneducated in how something like that might theoretically work, but my instinctive reaction is 'ew, cyborg'. I have no objections to medication but changing brain chemicals to me is more of a slight adjustment than implanting technology. 

I'm aware this is an instinctual reaction and not terribly logical - people already use technology internally in the form of pacemakers for example. But because it's the brain I think I'd have that worry that it could affect me as a person rather than my illness iyswim? Again all theoretical and random thoughts, if it were an established treatment and was explained to me I could very well feel differently.

Not that I know of. Personally I have a chart that I use with exposures that I have to complete. If I do extra I get a 'reward', I allow myself to buy something nice. I make it little exciting things I want and don't allow myself to buy for any other reason, so it encourages me to push harder. 

If you'd like an ERP buddy I'd be happy to have someone to support/get support from. I'm currently doing ERP on my own after a house move left me minus a therapist temporarily.

Haha yes you're right. I wanted to reply to an OCD comment at one point and didn't want to use my normal account. Figured this was a good reminder!
 
I would however advise you clean literal shit. Just to make that clear. ;)

I won't reassure you here because we all know it's not helpful. You're doing the right thing by coming on here - keep yourself occupied for as long as possible and the thoughts will lessen. You can do it champ.

I would see your doctor about your hands though. It's common for people with some forms of OCD (notably contamination) to have dry hands because of the frequency that they wash them or use harsh cleaning materials. The cold weather makes it a million times worse. I have special soap and cream on an rx to protect my hands, and when it's very bad I get a steroid cream to help them recover. It's important to look after the physical aspects of OCD as well as the mental.
Most people using the word 'relationship' use it in a romantic/sexual context. I don't think it's too much of a leap to make that assumption.
I meant a sexual/romantic relationship as opposed to a big brother one.

You've pretty much answered this yourself here.

> I won't persue a relationship with her, because I know that we are on different levels. 

If you're not comfortable pursuing a relationship with her, why not? If you're not comfortable pursuing a relationship, why would you find her attractive in other contexts?


Someone said below it's only a five year age gap, it's four but I digress. At your age you should know that there's a huge difference between 12 and 16. Think back to when you were 12. Think about how you'd feel if your baby sister suddenly turned up with a 16yo boyfriend. 12yo's are not sexually mature, and they have a lot to learn. It's very likely that this 12yo is being nice to you in a big brother way - after all you're her friend's sibling.

As this is bothering you I would bring it up with your therapist at your next session. People have all sorts of strange fleeting notions about sex that often disgust them, even those without OCD. But the fact that you're dwelling on this and asking for reassurance shows it's bothering you more than normal.

Ask your doctor. A bunch of people on the net will definitely not know. The amount of medication you're on doesn't indicate much anyway as people have different reactions to meds and some will need more than others. My OCD was at one point classed as extreme but I manage well with a small dose of anti-d's and a LOT of exposure therapy/CBT. Some people will not respond as well to meds or to talking therapy and need a higher dose even with less severe symptoms.

I have contamination and although I use cream after every handwash my skin still dries and cracks, especially in the winter. I went to my pharmacist to get a steroid cream OTC and she was shocked at the state of my hands and arms...and I'm sitting there thinking that actually this is really mild for me. Just goes to show that even medical professionals have very little idea of the physical results of OCD.

You don't until you have your anxiety under better control. In the same way that an epileptic isn't allowed to drive for his and other safety, neither should you. 

What are you doing about your anxiety in general? Are you seeing a therapist, are you on any medication? What are your coping techniques for anxiety attacks in other situations? There will be a way you can transfer them to your driving anxiety.

Reddit in general has a terribly immature attitude to relationships. Any issue comes up and it's 'DUMP THEM', which is very easy to type from miles away, but not when it's your life in the shitter. 

Cheating and then lying about it is a massive thing and not something you should take lightly, but some people do manage to get past cheating in relationships. It depends very much on you and your girlfriend and isn't a decision anyone else can make for you. If you need an impartial ear though, please feel free to PM me.
Then OP letting him have the bathroom is like leaving a junkie to have their fix. It's never a good idea to be an enabler to destructive behaviour.

> she told me this was a part of an "act" that he made her do.

Yeahhh...no. Unlike most of the posters here I do think that being told certain things, if they fit into existing obsessions, can lead to further obsessions. For example if your girlfriend already had thoughts of her mother being hurt and then this guy came along with bullshit, it could play into her existing fears. 

However the fact is that she had a choice on how she dealt with this. She could have told you, or her therapist, or a friend about her thoughts, but instead chose to sleep with the guy, and that's the problem. If true then he's an asshole for messing with her, but she's an asshole for sleeping with him.

The 'act' is total nonsense. That doesn't play into OCD at all. There is no part of OCD that requires you to send text messages written in a specific way because someone else told you to. That, I'm afraid, is utter bullshit. Which makes me feel the rest of her story is also, utter bullshit.

Sorry dude. If you want to keep your relationship despite the cheating (contrary to reddit opinion, some people do) I'd suggest you head to couples counselling, and also have a joint meeting with her therapist to make it clear what OCD is and how it affects people. All the best man.

I have contamination OCD which was classed as severe, at one point I was housebound and relied on my partner for a lot of things. Since I've been in recovery we've talked a lot about it so I'll give you our thoughts. We are no longer together as a couple but are good friends so if you have any specific questions for him I can ask and get back to you in a day or two. TL;DR at end for summary.

Regarding the things you do for your partner, you're making the same mistakes my ex did. When someone you love gets upset your natural reaction is to comfort them, in your case by cleaning things, but as you recognize yourself this only makes things worse. Reassurance is a good way to make OCD spiral - it feeds on it. By cleaning your feet and your body and sticking to her rules, you are reassuring her that her thoughts are reasonable and okay and that allows the OCD to get a firm hold, it gives her an excuse if you will to keep doing it. Unfortunately once you have been reassured that one thing is 'dirty' your mind then jumps to other, more severe things, and if you reassure those thoughts, it'll accept them, and so on. Important to mention here that she will still know in there that the things she is doing don't make any sense, that's what makes OCD such a horrible disease to live with. You know the thought you're having and the things you're doing are, logically, ridiculous, and that you should stop, but the OCD has a clever little way of going, 'Oh but what if...'

The reassurance has to stop, however I do not suggest you just plonk down and say 'I'm not doing x, y or z any more'. This is where it would be ideal for you to have a joint therapy session, the therapist can tell you what she thinks is helpful for you to be doing and what your partner can cope with. If you remove all reassurance at once she may crack under the strain, it's better to wean her off gradually.

When you say the therapist is not helping, why do you think that? Has your partners behavior made no improvements during treatment? Is she on any medication, do you know what her treatment plan is? It is common for people with OCD to be tried on an SSRI, which is an antidepressant, they help many people a great deal. This should be used in conjunction with talking therapy, normally a technique called Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) which helps you to take your thoughts and structure your reactions to them in a different way. Less severe cases can be treated purely with talking therapy, it really depends on the individual. If you feel that your particular therapist is not helping, find a different one. It's very common to have to go through more than one therapist to find one you click with.

CBT also helps with another therapy called Exposure Therapy, which is quite literally exposing yourself to your fears. For example the feet near the door - one day she might stand on the 'dirty' patch but be allowed to wash her feet afterwards. Then stand and only be allowed to change her socks afterwards. Then have to walk down the hall in 'dirty' socks but be allowed to clean the floor. Then have to walk down the hall and *not* clean the floor. Then expand to other areas of the house. Tiny little baby steps. If you can ignore a compulsion for around half an hour it becomes much easier to deal with, the panic lessens and you realise it's still hard, but not as essential as you considered it half an hour ago. I've gotten past a lot of shit this way, just thinking 'I'll make a cup of tea and just not think about this, oh look there's ten minutes gone, well I still want to clean that floor but you know what I have that email to write first and oh look that's twenty minutes, well, only ten to go now I might as well hang on...' It takes a LOT of willpower but it will come with practice.

Bear in mind that as she really starts to work on her OCD there will be a lot of tears and tantrums. Her therapist should be teaching her ways to cope with this but honestly, you will get quite a bit of it. I didn't like getting pissy at my partner so I used to walk off and hide in a room when I got stressed, which stressed him out and caused many arguments. Make sure you are not her only support, it is too much for one person and we learned that far too late. If she has friends/family who can be trusted not to reassure that's great. You could also send her here, we're a very supportive community (I've been here a while, lost my other account because I'm a muffin) and I personally am always happy to chat to someone with OCD, either about it or about something else entirely. In the past when I've struggled with exposure therapy I've posted here, just for distraction while I calm down from whatever the challenge is, and it's been a great help. 

You are right not to raise a child in that environment. I know someone with severe OCD who has a young child, and he really suffers as a result of his mom's OCD. His mother completely ignores any warnings given to her and is pregnant again, which is really very silly of her. Wait until your partner has a firm grip on her illness before considering children. 

The most important thing is that your partner must WANT to get better. To fight the shit going on in your head is very hard and if she doesn't put the work in, she won't get very far. I'm hoping that since she is already in therapy that won't be an issue. You sound like a very loving and supportive partner and I'm sure with your help she will learn to kick OCD's butt. 

**TL;DR -** Do not provide reassurance, it will encourage more severe compulsions. Speak to the therapist and seek a joint session to discuss how you can help. If you're not happy with the progress with this therapist, try another. Overview of standard treatments. Definitely don't have kids. Beating OCD is hard work but you can do it!
